No t e s
1. 
The Presumption of Reviewability. Justice Marshall cited Abbott Labs 
V. Gardner, 387 U.S. 136 (1967), a case that we will discuss in more detail in 
the next chapter, for the proposition that actions of administrators are 
presumed to be judicially reviewable. Justice Marshall also rejected the 
argument that the petitioners were not entitled to judicial review because 
section 701(a)(2) of the APA does not authorize such review when “agency 
action is committed to agency discretion by law.” Again, we will explore that 
provision in more detail in the next chapter. For now, simply observe that 
Overton Park entertained a challenge by a group of citizens, who as individuals 
apparently had a stake in the routing of the highway, to an administrative 
determination for which Congress had prescribed no procedures and which, as 
a matter of custom, resulted in no formal documentation or written 
explanation. Nor had Congress anywhere specifically authorized judicial 
review of such decisions.
2. 
Requiring an Informal Record. According to Overton Park, the 
conclusion that judicial review is appropriate necessitates some sort of “record” 
on which to conduct the review. The Court rejected rehance on “post hoc” 
htigation affidavits, instead requiring review of the “ ‘whole record’ compiled 
by the agency.” But to be sure, if the Federal Highway Administration were 
simply to dump on the District Court all of the paperwork relating to the 
planning, design, approval, and construction of 1-40 through Memphis, the 
judge would be buried and soon lost. Hence, the Supreme Court required an 
explanation with some “findings” by the Secretary in order to structure judicial 
evaluation of the underlying record. The Secretary’s decision and “rationale” 
could then be tested against the material in the record.
The requirement of a “record” for judicial review likely has predictable 
impheations for the administrative process. Any official who knows that his or 
her action will be tested by reference to a record will likely build one to support 
the decision that is made, should htigation arise in the future. This requires 
the development of administrative routines that can be fohowed by 
subordinates—^in this case the federal district engineers and the Federal 
Highway Administration—^to assure that appropriate information is 
assembled on the crucial questions of feasibihty and prudence. The prospect of 
judicial review thus reinforces the bureaucratization of those agency functions 
that it touches.
